name: PT Saraswanti Anugerah Makmur, Tbk

frontmatter.title: Saraswanti Anugerah Makmur — a working-capital cycle the price does not discount
frontmatter.summary: SAMF formulates premium NPK compounds for Indonesian plantations and grew sales through a hard year. The growth was funded on the balance sheet: inventory and receivables absorbed the profit, operating cash flow turned negative, the revolver was drawn to more than double short-term debt, and free cash flow to the firm was -485.2 while a dividend of 107.6 was declared. At Rp270 the stock capitalises a steady compounder. We initiate at SELL.
thesis: The price pays for a compounder, the accounts show a working-capital cycle. Nine-month operating cash flow of -657 IDR bn against profit of 189 IDR bn, inventories at 1,745 IDR bn against 867 IDR bn at the prior year-end and short-term bank loans at 1,548 IDR bn are not the profile of a business compounding free cash [S5].

Growth is real but it is being bought with debt, not earned in cash. Nine-month sales rose to 3,274 IDR bn from 2,924 IDR bn, yet the revolver funded the stock and the receivables, so the free cash flow to the firm we forecast for FY2026E is -485.2 [S5].

The margin is stable, not cyclical-lucky. Gross margin held at 21.3% in FY2025 and 21.4% in the nine months of 2026, so we capitalise the last actual rather than the wider spread of FY2023-FY2024 [S4, S5].

Policy and scale run against the non-subsidised formulator: the subsidised ceiling was cut to 92,000 IDR per 50kg sack and Pupuk Indonesia plans to lift NPK capacity from 4.6 m t to 5.9 m t by 2030 [S7, S10].
Our DCF returns Rp186 against Rp270; a 20.0% liquidity haircut takes the target to Rp177, -29.9% of downside [S5].

blocks.text: Saraswanti Anugerah Makmur formulates NPK compound fertilisers and sells them, for the most part, to oil-palm estates rather than through the subsidised channel [S4]. We initiate coverage at SELL with a target of Rp177, -29.9% from the Rp270 price, after a 20.0% haircut applied to a weighted value of Rp222 [S5, S4]. The rating is not a call on the franchise, which is a competent, profitable formulator with a long dividend record; it is a call on the price, which capitalises the franchise as though the cash conversion problem of the last four quarters did not exist [S5].

What the market pays is visible in the multiples. At Rp270 the shares trade on 9.6x our FY2026E earnings and 1.4x our forecast book value, with a dividend yield of 4.4% on the payout we assume [S5, S4]. Those are multiples for a steady staples compounder. What the accounts deliver is different: nine-month operating cash flow of -657 IDR bn against a profit of 189 IDR bn, inventories of 1,745 IDR bn against 867 IDR bn at the prior year-end, and short-term bank loans of 1,548 IDR bn [S5]. The company sold more and collected less, and it funded the gap with a revolver rather than with its own cash.

Our variant view is therefore not on the sales line. Sales grew to 3,274 IDR bn in the nine months from 2,924 IDR bn a year earlier, and the company's own plan is for more [S5, S6]. Our difference is about quality and funding: growth of that kind, at a working-capital intensity near 56.6% of sales, consumes cash before it returns any, and this company pays out roughly half of its profit while doing it [S5, S4]. Free cash flow to the firm is -485.2 in FY2026E. The model's free cash flow to equity is 331.3, but it is positive only because the 871.8 of net borrowing is counted as an inflow; strike that draw out and the equity cash flow is negative. It is also struck before the 107.6 parent dividend, which the engine does not deduct, so the dividend is funded from the revolver rather than from the year's cash generation. That is why the dividend and the debt build cannot both continue on the same trajectory [S5].

Three things move the value. The first is gross margin, where the last two years have run at essentially the same level and where we assume no recovery [S5, S4]. The second is working capital: if the September stock and receivables are a seasonal peak that unwinds in the fourth quarter, the cash flow picture repairs itself without any change in the trading; if they are the new normal, the revolver stays drawn and the interest bill rises [S5]. The third is the payout, which the board held near half of profit through the cycle and which we do not assume is raised [S4]. We weight the DCF at 60%, EV/EBITDA at 25% and P/E at 15%, and we show the gap between the primary method and the EBITDA cross-check rather than smoothing it away [S5].

Indonesian compound fertiliser sits in two markets at once. The subsidised market is planned, allocated and price-capped, and it is served overwhelmingly by the state-owned producer group. The non-subsidised market is commercial: estates and plantations buy formulated compounds with specific nutrient ratios, trace elements and coating, and they buy them from private formulators who compete on agronomy advice, delivery and brand rather than on the price of the underlying nutrients. A formulator's cost base is imported phosphate and potash plus nitrogen intermediates, so the business is a converter of globally priced nutrients into a branded, applied product. That structure matters for valuation: there is no mining cost curve to own, only a formulation and service advantage that has to be defended every season.

SAMF is a fertiliser specialist with a single operating segment: the manufacture and sale of NPK compound fertilisers, principally for oil palm, with a smaller book of non-palm plantation customers [S4]. Maximum production capacity is 700,000 t a year and actual output was 581,099 t in FY2025 against 607,593 t in FY2024, so the company ran at a little over four fifths of its installed line in the last financial year [S4]. That is the single most important operating fact in the file, because it means the next increment of volume does not need a new plant; it needs demand [S4].

The product range is built around granulated NPK compounds sold under the FERTINDO, PUPINDO and PHONIKA brands, with dedicated oil-palm formulations that combine macro and micronutrients with humic and fulvic acids [S4]. The technology the company emphasises is melt granulation and coating, which it argues makes its products more efficient per kilogram applied than simple blends [S4]. This is a formulation business, not a commodity chemical plant: the value added is in the recipe, the granule and the advice that goes with it, and the raw materials are bought in [S4].

The customer base is broad for a company of its size: more than 500 customers, most of them in the oil-palm sector, served through marketing offices across Sumatra, Java and Kalimantan [S4]. That breadth is a real asset in a downturn, because no single estate group can take the year with it, but it also explains the receivables: a long tail of plantation customers buying on terms is a structurally working-capital-hungry book [S5, S4]. The company describes its customers as plantation companies and cooperatives rather than distributors, which puts the credit risk directly on the formulator's balance sheet [S4].

Group structure is simple and tightly held. The operating business sits in three subsidiaries that are almost wholly owned, and PT Saraswanti Utama holds 74.3% of the listed company [S4]. Minority interests are small and stable, and there is no holding-company layer between the controller and the listed entity that the filings disclose [S4]. The shares were split in February 2025, a change in the count rather than in the capital [S4].

Strategy, as disclosed, is unexciting and credible: hold the premium oil-palm franchise, broaden the product range beyond palm, modernise the plants and digitise the sales and agronomy process [S4]. The only growth project in the accounts is land management and site works at Tanjung Buton, a project still at the preparation stage rather than a funded plant [S4]. There is no announced capacity expansion, no acquisition and no rights issue, which is why our forecast keeps capex at maintenance levels and adds no volume beyond the existing line [S4, S5].

The cost structure is the whole story of the margin. Raw and auxiliary materials were 2,880 IDR bn in FY2025 against sales of 4,075.0, the dominant line by a wide margin, and those materials are imported phosphate, potash and nitrogen intermediates bought on the spot market rather than mined or produced in house [S4, S10]. A formulator with an imported basket and an unhedged buying policy is long the nutrient cycle and short the rupiah, and both exposures show up in the gross margin before they show up anywhere else [S4, S11].

The addressable market is large and growing slowly. Indonesian compound fertiliser consumption was about 3.0 m t at the end of 2024, while the company estimates the plantation sector's potential need for urea and NPK together at 15.5 m t a year, of which oil palm accounts for roughly 65.0% [S4]. The gap between consumption and potential need is the company's long-run argument: estates are under-fertilising relative to agronomic requirements, and a recovery in palm economics would close some of that gap [S4]. That argument is directionally right and it is also the reason the current cycle hurts, because under-fertilising is exactly what happens when growers cannot afford the bag [S8].

Competition is concentrated at the top and fragmented below it. The company counts 7.0 producers of meaningful scale in Indonesia and puts its own share of national non-subsidised NPK supply at about 5.0% [S4]. The dominant competitor is the state-owned Pupuk Indonesia group, which is expanding NPK capacity from 4.6 m t today to a targeted 5.9 m t by 2030 [S10]. That is a large increment against a national compound-fertiliser market that consumed about 3.0 m t at the end of 2024, and it is the single largest structural threat to a private formulator's spread [S10, S4].

Policy has moved against the commercial price umbrella. The government cut the subsidised NPK retail ceiling by a fifth to 92,000 IDR per 50kg sack from 22 October 2025, explicitly to lower farmers' costs [S7]. A cheaper subsidised bag pulls demand away from the premium commercial product at the margin, and it compresses the price a private formulator can charge for a comparable analysis [S7, S4]. At the same time, the farm-gate evidence shows that growers outside the subsidised allocation were paying sharply more, not less: oil-palm smallholders in Bangka reported urea and compound prices rising by large steps in the first half of 2026 and fertiliser absorbing close to half of monthly income [S8]. The two facts together describe a market where the subsidised price is administratively low and the commercial price is set by import cost, which is exactly the spread SAMF lives on [S7, S8].

The supply side is import-dependent and exposed to shipping and geopolitics. Indonesia does not mine its own phosphate and potash at scale; even the state producer is scouting phosphate and potash assets abroad, including in Russia, to secure feedstock [S10]. When the Iran-US confrontation escalated in mid-2026, the immediate channel of transmission into Indonesian agriculture was exactly this one: phosphate and liquid nitrogen imports from the Persian Gulf, and with them the cost of every compound on the market [S11]. A formulator cannot hedge that, and its customers cannot absorb it quickly, so the cost lands in the margin and then in the receivables [S11, S5].

On the five-forces view, buyer power is high and rising: plantation customers are professional, price-aware, and have the subsidised alternative in front of them [S4, S7]. Supplier power is high because the nutrient basket is imported and concentrated in a few origins [S10, S11]. Rivalry is moderate among the private formulators and severe against the state group's scale [S4, S10]. New entry is possible, since granulation is not capital-intensive at small scale, but brand, registration and agronomy service raise the bar [S4]. Substitutes are the subsidised single-nutrient and compound products and, at the margin, reduced fertilisation itself [S8].

The moat, honestly assessed, is narrow. SAMF has no position on a global cost curve and no resource it owns; its advantage is formulation know-how, an oil-palm-specific brand and a service network built over decades [S4]. That is enough to earn a stable gross margin in a normal year, which the company has done, but it is not enough to resist a subsidised price cut or a state capacity expansion on its own [S4, S7, S10]. It is a good business inside a policy-shaped market, and it should be valued as such.

The reported record is one of growth in revenue and erosion in margin. Sales rose from 3,689.4 in FY2022 to 4,075.0 in FY2025, but gross margin slipped from 24.0% to 21.3% and earnings per share from 39.6 to 24.9 [S0, S4]. The FY2025 result was the weak year: revenue grew while attributable profit fell and the dividend was cut to 10.5 a share, 108 IDR bn in total, from the 19.0 paid for FY2024 [S4, S5]. Return on equity fell from 33.6% in FY2023 to 15.3% in FY2025, which is what a stable margin on a growing asset base and a rising debt load will do [S0].

One restatement had to be made before the model could be trusted. The data pack's depreciation line carries only the general and administrative charge, whereas the financial statements show total depreciation of 42.7 IDR bn in FY2025 and 35.5 IDR bn in FY2024, most of it sitting in cost of goods sold [S4]. We restated the historical D&A and the cash flow build on the audited figures, and we use a forecast charge of 1.1% of sales, consistent with the 36.3 IDR bn booked in the first nine months of 2026 [S5, S4]. Capex is modest and has been below depreciation in the last year: 61.8 IDR bn of cash capex in FY2025 after the heavy year in FY2024 that completed the capacity expansion [S4].

The 2026 trading pattern is the core of the analysis. The first quarter was poor: sales of 601 IDR bn, down sharply year on year, with operating cash flow negative and profit lower [S9]. The second quarter then recovered strongly, and the nine-month totals show sales of 3,274 IDR bn against 2,924 IDR bn, growth of about a tenth, with profit of 189 IDR bn essentially flat against the prior year [S5]. The most likely reconciliation, and it is our reading rather than a company statement, is production running ahead of sales: the company built finished goods through the first half and carried them into the second, so cost went through the profit and loss before revenue did [S5]. Inventory tells that story plainly, at 1,745 IDR bn against 867 IDR bn at the prior year-end, with finished goods the larger part of the balance [S5].

That build was funded with debt. Short-term bank loans reached 1,548 IDR bn at the end of September against a modest cash balance of 236 IDR bn, and the nine-month operating cash flow was -657 IDR bn against a positive figure a year earlier [S5]. Inventory days have lengthened materially and receivable days have risen with them, so the working-capital cycle, not the trading margin, is where the cash went [S5]. The company has the banking lines to carry it: the disclosed facilities price working-capital credit in the high sevens and investment credit a little above that, with letter-of-credit and trust-receipt lines on top [S5]. That is a reasonable cost of carry, and it is still a cost: nine-month finance expense was substantial and we annualise it at roughly 8.5% on gross debt [S5].

Our forecast reproduces the last actual and then grows it. FY2026E revenue of 4,498.8 is a tenth above FY2025, built from the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter that sells into the stock the company is carrying, and it sits between the run-rate and the company's own plan for growth of 7.0% or more, the low end of its guided range [S5, S6]. Gross margin is held at 21.4%, the nine-month actual, and at roughly that level thereafter; we do not restore the wider spread of FY2023 and FY2024 [S5, S4]. Operating expenses are held at about 11.4% of sales, between the FY2025 and nine-month 2026 ratios, and the tax rate is the statutory one [S4, S5]. On those inputs the model produces FY2026E EBITDA of 499.4 and net profit attributable to shareholders of 287.1, with earnings per share of 28.0 [S5].

Cash is where the forecast diverges from the earnings. We rebuild the year from the September actual rather than from the December 2025 balance sheet: operating working capital reached its reported September level, and we carry that stock into the year-end instead of assuming a fourth-quarter release nobody has sourced, which is 56.6% of FY2026E sales [S5, F15, F16]. At that intensity the incremental working capital in FY2026E is 822.6, exactly the build already incurred in the first nine months, and free cash flow to the firm is -485.2 [S5]. The engine's free cash flow to equity line is 331.3: positive only because the 871.8 of net borrowing is an inflow, and struck before the 107.6 parent dividend, because the engine deducts only minority dividends. Before that draw the equity cash flow is negative, so the dividend is paid out of the revolver rather than out of the year's cash generation [S5]. The forecast debt line now carries every interest-bearing obligation, not just the revolver: short-term bank loans of 1,548 IDR bn plus current maturities of bank loans of 29.9 IDR bn and finance leases of 3.8 IDR bn, plus non-current bank loans of 62.0 IDR bn and finance leases of 2.3 IDR bn, which is 1,645.5 of gross debt against 328.6 of cash and a net-debt line of 1,316.9 [S5]. That net-debt line is a year-end projection, not the September stock: the September accounts report net debt on the same full basis - short-term bank loans of 1,548 IDR bn plus current maturities of 29.9 IDR bn and 3.8 IDR bn plus non-current bank loans of 62.0 IDR bn and finance leases of 2.3 IDR bn, less cash of 236 IDR bn - which is higher than the year-end projection by the fourth-quarter cash generation the forecast assumes [S5]. The DCF's own equity bridge is kept on the 30 June balance sheet, the date from which its stub starts, and the difference by which the September net debt exceeds that bridge is disclosed rather than mixed into a flow that begins three months earlier [S5]. Rebuilding the year on the actual stock, rather than on a ratio that implied an unstated fourth-quarter release, cuts the DCF value per share to Rp186 from the level the previous draft carried, and the target with it. This is the arithmetic behind the rating: a company paying out part of its profit while its working capital grows by 822.6 is funding the dividend from the bank [S5].

The balance sheet carries three things the headline ratios hide. First, related-party trade payables of 284 IDR bn, 11.1% of total liabilities at the end of September, mostly owed to the controller's trading arm, which is a legitimate sourcing arrangement and also a governance fact that deserves a discount rather than a benefit of the doubt [S5]. Second, an upward land revaluation of 265 IDR bn booked through other comprehensive income in FY2025, which raised book equity without adding a rupiah of earning power; the price-to-book multiple therefore flatters the stock and the return on equity understates the operating return [S4]. Third, the interest convention in our model charges interest on opening debt, so FY2026E interest of 65.8 is below what the company is already paying: nine months of finance expense were 76.7 IDR bn, an annualised run-rate well above it, and the fourth quarter alone on the drawn gross debt is a further charge at the effective rate [S5]. The gap is about a tenth of FY2026E earnings, and it flatters the fourth-quarter cash generation that reconciles the year-end net-debt projection of 1,316.9 to the September full-basis stock by roughly the same amount; it is a timing convention that reverses from FY2027E, when the charge is 139.9 on the drawn debt [S5]. The valuation's net debt is taken from the 30 June balance-sheet date in the pack, the same date the DCF's stub starts, and the September full-basis net debt is disclosed in the paragraph above [S5]. Both conventions make the forecast slightly optimistic, and neither changes the direction of the call [S5].

Earnings quality, read against the flags we are required to test, is acceptable on governance and poor on cash conversion. The three-year audited trend is the right starting point, because the card says the trend matters more than the level. In FY2023 profit of 420.1 compared with operating cash flow of 77.4 IDR bn, on total assets that opened at 3,098 IDR bn and closed at 2,794 IDR bn; in FY2024 profit of 396.8 against operating cash flow of 314 IDR bn, on total assets that closed at 2,788 IDR bn from 2,794 IDR bn; and in FY2025 profit of 267.5 against operating cash flow of 313 IDR bn, on total assets that closed at 3,175 IDR bn from 2,788 IDR bn [S4][S12]. Measured as profit less operating cash flow over average total assets, the accruals ratio was in double digits in FY2023, fell to low single digits in FY2024 and turned negative in FY2025: earnings outran cash once, then converted cleanly for two years [S4][S12]. The 2026 break is therefore a break in the trend, not a persistent pattern: nine-month profit of 189 IDR bn against operating cash flow of -657 IDR bn on total assets of 4,528 IDR bn is a swing no operating margin explains, and it is the single clearest earnings-quality flag in the file [S5]. We classify it optics-class rather than manipulation-class: it is disclosed, measurable and consistent with a working-capital cycle, and the fourth quarter is the test. The inventory build is the same flag in stock form — finished goods of 1,051 IDR bn at the end of September, more than the entire inventory balance of 867 IDR bn at the prior year-end — and it is optics-class too, but the company has not explained it: the interim accounts carry no management commentary on the inventory note, and the nearest sourced statement is that the company secures raw materials around ordering windows against production targets [S6], which speaks to raw-material timing, not to the finished-goods stock. Our reading, and it is an interpretation rather than a company statement, is production timing ahead of the fourth-quarter selling season; the fourth quarter is the test of it [S5]. On notation, the FY2025 annual report discloses no administrative sanction from the capital-market authority or any other regulator and no restatement, and neither the annual report nor the September accounts disclose a special-monitoring board listing; the shares are listed and traded normally [S4, S5]. Related-party exposure is a purchasing channel, not a sales channel: the balances are trade payables to the controller's trading arm, 11.1% of liabilities and nil per cent of revenue, which we classify optics-class but governance-relevant [S5]. The land revaluation of 265 IDR bn through other comprehensive income is optics-class on the card's definition — aggressive but disclosed — and it affects book value, not earnings [S4]. We find no manipulation-class flag: no restatement history, no qualified opinion, no change of auditor and no special notation appears in the filings [S4, S5].

SAMF is a converter of imported nutrients, not a resource owner, so the commodity-cyclical method card's instruction to anchor on a sourced through-cycle commodity price cannot be applied to a metal or an energy series. What it can be applied to is the spread: a normalised gross margin on a normalised volume. We therefore run a discounted cash flow on free cash flow to the firm as the primary method, using the last actual margin rather than a recovered one, and we use EV/EBITDA and P/E as cross-checks against the trading history [S5, S4]. The weights are 60% for the DCF, 25% for EV/EBITDA and 15% for P/E, because the DCF is the only method that charges the company for the working capital it actually consumes [S5].

The cost of capital is the house build, and we state it in full so the reader can reproduce it. The Indonesian risk-free rate is 7.4%; the house subtracts the sovereign default spread of 1.6% before applying the equity premium, because the rupiah risk-free rate embeds a sovereign credit risk that the mature-market premium does not. The mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2% and the country risk premium is 2.5% [S0]. The industry beta, relevered for the company's capital structure, gives a levered beta of 1.28, so the cost of equity is 7.4% less 1.6% plus 1.28 times the sum of 4.2% and 2.5%, which is 14.4% [S0]. Pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% is the house market cost of debt, the risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread rather than the rate the disclosed facilities carry: the Mandiri working-capital lines price in the high sevens, and the effective charge on the drawn debt is 8.5%, which is what the interest line uses [S5, S0]. Taxed at the statutory rate, and at market weights of 64.7% equity and 35.3% debt, the weighted average cost of capital is 11.9% [S5, S0]. The beta is an industry default rather than a measured regression, which is a weakness of the build we accept: with a thin and concentrated shareholder register the measured beta would be dominated by the controlling holder's liquidity, not by the operating risk [S4].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of 3,027.5 and an equity value of Rp186 per share, with 57.1% of that value in the terminal period [S5]. A terminal share of that size is high, and it is the honest consequence of a business whose invested capital grows with sales: the explicit forecast years are largely a working-capital funding exercise, and the value sits in the years after the balance sheet stops expanding. We have tested the rate and the terminal growth inside the house bounds rather than adjusting them to fit a target [S0].

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative rather than embarrassing. At 6.3 times EBITDA the EBITDA method gives Rp175 a share, -6.3% below the DCF, because EBITDA is the wrong earnings measure for this company: it ignores the 822.6 of working capital that growth consumes, and the equity bridge at the valuation date subtracts a net debt that is materially larger than the one the forecast path ends with [S5]. One mechanical point is disclosed rather than buried: the DCF carries a bridge item for the working capital already spent by 30 June and therefore already inside the June net debt, which the FY2026E full-year flow would otherwise charge twice, and the engine applies the same single bridge to the EBITDA cross-check, where it does not belong; the EBITDA method's own net debt is the June figure and its value on that basis is lower than the number shown [S5, F15]. The P/E cross-check applies 8.9 times FY2025A attributable earnings, the last audited year and the metric the engine actually uses, and gives Rp223, 19.6% from the DCF [S5]. We keep the multiple on the audited year rather than on our own FY2026E forecast because a peer multiple applied to our forecast would capitalise our estimate twice; the FY2026E earnings are shown separately in the multiples table, where the price implies 9.6x [S5, S4]. We weight the DCF highest precisely because the other two methods are blind to the cash conversion problem that is the thesis [S5].

The reverse DCF does not have a solution in this case, and we report that rather than forcing one. At working capital of 56.6% of sales, no revenue growth rate inside the tested band produces a discounted value near the Rp270 price, because additional growth destroys value before it creates any: each extra rupiah of sales needs working capital ahead of it, and the company pays out half its profit while funding that need with debt [S5]. The absence of a solution is itself the finding. The price cannot be explained by any plausible growth path on these margins and this working-capital intensity; it can only be explained by an expectation that the working-capital ratio falls back toward the FY2024 level, or that the margin widens beyond anything the last two years delivered [S5, S4]. Both are possible; neither is what we forecast.

The final step is liquidity. The stock's three-month average daily traded value is below the fund's lowest liquidity floor, which is the bucket that carries the house's 20.0% haircut; the smaller names that carry a tenth trade several times our turnover, so the difference is the grid, not a view on SAMF [S5]. We apply it explicitly, as its own line, rather than smuggling it into the discount rate. That takes the weighted value of Rp222 to a fundamental target of Rp177, which is the Rp177 we publish, and it takes the scenario-weighted return to -29.9% [S5]. The haircut is not a comment on the company's quality; it is the price of getting out of a position in a name with a thin free float and a controlling shareholder [S4].

The method card's output contract, adapted to a formulator with no resource to value, is met as follows. There is no through-cycle commodity price to anchor, so the DCF is run on the last actual margin and volume and the NAV per share is Rp186; at spot prices the same model is the same number, because the margin is already the spot-year actual rather than a normalised one, and that is the honest limitation of a spread business [S5]. The dividend-capacity anchor the market uses for this name is visible: at the modelled payout the shares yield 4.4% on our FY2026E dividend, below the yield the price would need to justify the cash conversion we forecast [S5, S4]. Leverage is the risk metric the balance sheet now owns: net debt is 2.6 times FY2026E EBITDA, and at trough EBITDA the same debt is roughly twice that multiple, which is the constraint on the dividend rather than the payout ratio [S5]. We state plainly that the market is anchoring on dividend capacity and on the trailing multiple, and that we are valuing the cash flow that can fund it. The macro tilt sits against the name on both counts: the house macro deck has the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD to the dollar in FY2027E against Rp16,448/USD in FY2025, a cost headwind for an importer of phosphate and potash that buys unhedged, and the deck's stance on the commodity bloc is neutral while Indonesian oil-import beneficiaries are avoided, which is the wrong side of the tilt for a company whose raw-material basket is imported and dollar-priced [S10, S11].

The largest risk is the customer's economics, not the company's. Oil-palm smallholders and estates are the demand base, and when fresh-fruit-bunch prices are weak relative to fertiliser cost they cut application rates before they cut anything else [S8]. The reporting from Bangka in the first half of 2026 is the clearest evidence available: growers paying substantially more for urea and compound while their own output price did not keep pace, with fertiliser taking close to half of monthly income [S8]. A demand base under that much pressure is a demand base that can defer a season, and a deferred season is a lost sale rather than a delayed one [S8].

The second risk is the imported nutrient basket and the rupiah. Phosphate and potash are imported, and the state producer's own search for mines abroad including in Russia underlines how little of the chain is domestic [S10]. When the Iran-US confrontation escalated, the transmission channel into Indonesian agriculture was named explicitly as phosphate and liquid nitrogen imports from the Persian Gulf [S11]. A formulator buying spot, unhedged, and selling forward to estates carries the timing mismatch between cost and price, and the FY2026 record shows the mismatch landing in working capital as well as in margin [S11, S5].

The third risk is policy and state capacity. The subsidised NPK ceiling was cut to 92,000 IDR per 50kg sack from 22 October 2025, which lowers the reference price for every compound sold beside it [S7]. Pupuk Indonesia plans to lift NPK capacity from 4.6 m t to 5.9 m t by 2030 [S10]. If that capacity is built and used, the commercial spread compresses at exactly the moment SAMF's own line is already running below its maximum, and the volume growth in our base case becomes harder to earn [S4, S10].

The fourth risk is liquidity, and it is the one the market is least prepared for because it is new. A nine-month operating cash flow of -657 IDR bn, inventory at 1,745 IDR bn and short-term bank loans at 1,548 IDR bn is a balance sheet that depends on the revolver being renewed [S5]. The company has adequate facilities today, and the disclosed pricing is not distressed, but a working-capital line that doubles in nine months is a covenant and renewal risk that did not exist a year ago [S5]. If the fourth quarter does not convert the finished goods into cash, the dividend becomes a financing decision rather than a distribution decision [S5].

The fifth risk is governance and related-party gravity. The controller holds 74.3%, free float is thin, and related-party payables of 284 IDR bn, 11.1% of liabilities, are owed to the controller's own trading arm [S4, S5]. Those purchases may well be at arm's length and on ordinary terms, and the disclosure is adequate, but a minority holder in a company that buys from its controlling shareholder at scale should require a discount for the possibility of terms that are merely defensible [S5]. The FY2025 land revaluation of 265 IDR bn through other comprehensive income, which lifted book value without lifting earnings, is a second reminder that the accounts are managed with an eye on the equity line [S4].

The sixth risk is that our most likely case is too cautious rather than too bold. We hold gross margin flat and assume no margin recovery, no volume beyond the existing line and no new plant [S4, S5]. If the palm cycle turns, the bull case is real: a margin restored to the FY2023 and FY2024 spread, growth above base on the spare capacity the line already has, and a working-capital unwind give a value of Rp316 and a target of Rp342 on the twelve-month roll, before the liquidity haircut. After the house 20.0% haircut the bull target is still above the Rp270 price, though by a narrow margin [S5, S4]. The bear is the mirror of that, plus one asymmetry we can source: a receivables impairment on the long tail of plantation customers, which is why the bear carries a charge the bull does not reverse [S8, S5]. A rights issue is the tail beyond the bear: if the revolver is not renewed on the same terms, the equity raise would dilute rather than impair, and we do not model it because no facility is disclosed as at risk [S5]. What we will not do is capitalise that turn before it appears in the fourth-quarter cash flow [S5].

The probabilities sum to one and are mirrored: 25% bear, 50% base and 25% bull. The core shocks are mirrored — revenue growth, gross margin and working-capital intensity move in opposite directions by the same amounts in each tail — so the base case is the centre rather than the cautious edge. Each tail carries one sourced asymmetry: the bear takes the receivables impairment, which the bull does not reverse, and the bull restores the payout, which the bear does not cut [S8, S4]. The base case value is Rp189 and the base target Rp204; the bear case is Rp121 and Rp136; the bull case is Rp316 and Rp342 [S5]. The bull case is worth Rp316 a share at the valuation date and Rp342 on the twelve-month roll, both before the liquidity haircut; the twelve-month roll is the horizon, not a haircut value. After the house 20.0% haircut the bull target remains above the Rp270 price, by a narrow margin, so the asymmetry does not run against the price in every scenario: the bull clears it, while the base and bear do not. The investment case we publish is the post-haircut target, because that is what a holder can realise; the pre-haircut figures are fundamental values [S5].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A positive operating cash flow in the fourth quarter and a fall in inventory below the September peak would tell us the build was seasonal, and we would raise the working-capital assumption and the target with it [S5]. A restored payout above half of profit with positive free cash flow would do the same [S4]. On the downside, a renewed increase in the subsidised ceiling, a commissioning date for the state producer's new NPK lines, or a further draw on the revolver without an inventory unwind would each take us toward the bear case [S7, S10, S5]. Palm fresh-fruit-bunch prices and estate replanting activity are the upstream variables to watch, because they lead our customers' buying decisions by a season [S8].

Ownership is concentrated and disclosed plainly. PT Saraswanti Utama holds 74.3% of the shares, the same holder has controlled the company since listing, and the free float is small enough that the stock's liquidity is a function of the controlling family's intentions rather than of the market's [S4]. The board and commissioners are named in the annual report and include independent commissioners, and the company states that neither it nor its subsidiaries, directors or commissioners were party to material litigation in FY2025 [S4]. It also states that no administrative sanction was received from the capital-market authority or any other regulator in FY2025 [S4].

The audit trail is clean on its face. The opinion reproduced in the annual report is unqualified, there has been no restatement of prior-year figures and no change of auditor disclosed, and the related-party disclosures are itemised by counterparty and by balance rather than aggregated into a single line [S4, S5]. None of that offsets the structural point: 11.1% of liabilities are owed to a related party, and the largest of those balances is owed to the controller's trading arm [S5]. A minority investor is effectively buying a share of a business whose raw-material sourcing runs through the controlling group, and the disclosure is the only protection available [S5].

The dividend record is the governance feature that has mattered most to holders. The company paid 15.0 for FY2022, 20.5 for FY2023 and 19.0 for FY2024 before cutting to 10.5 for FY2025, a total of 108 IDR bn declared at the AGMS of 18 June 2026 [S4, S5]. Part of that dividend was still unpaid to the controlling shareholders at the end of September, due by the end of the year: it is a related-party payable, a liability the company owes to its controllers, not a receivable owed to the company [S5]. A board that keeps paying through a working-capital squeeze is signalling confidence; it is also, in this instance, choosing the distribution over the deleveraging [S5].

On ESG, the exposures are those of the sector rather than of a specific controversy. The product is a fertiliser, so nutrient runoff and application efficiency are the material environmental questions, and the company's commercial argument for granulation and coating is partly an efficiency argument [S4]. The plants consume energy and the raw materials are imported over long distances, so the emissions profile is direct combustion at the granulation lines plus the embedded footprint of the nutrient basket [S4, S10]. On the social side, the customer base is plantation agriculture, which carries labour and land-use questions that the company does not control but is exposed to through its customers [S4]. No ESG-related enforcement, controversy or index exclusion is disclosed in the filings [S4].

The exchange's ownership regime has been tightening for companies with a dominant controlling holder. Minimum free-float requirements have been raised with staged deadlines, index providers have been reviewing the treatment of concentrated-ownership names, and the exchange has been publishing lists of companies whose shareholding concentration is high enough to warrant disclosure. For a company such as this one, sitting just inside the free-float rule, the practical consequences are index eligibility, passive demand and the discount that the market applies to any stock whose float can be absorbed by a single seller. None of that is a finding of wrongdoing; it is a liquidity and governance discount that belongs in the valuation, and we have applied it as a separate line rather than assuming it away.

The near-term calendar is dominated by cash, not by growth. The FY2025 dividend still owed to the controlling shareholders falls due by the end of 2026, and the year-end revolver position disclosed with the FY2026 accounts will show whether the September inventory converted [S5]. Any review of the subsidised NPK ceiling would move the reference price for the whole commercial market, and the direction of that review matters more than its timing [S7]. The FY2026 audited results, due in the first quarter of 2027, are the formal test of the working-capital explanation, and the AGMS in the second quarter is the first test of the payout after the cut [S5, S4].

Between updates we monitor a short list. Operating cash flow and the inventory balance each quarter, because they are the thesis [S5]. Short-term bank loans and finance expense, because they price the working-capital strategy [S5]. Gross margin, because it has been stable for two years and a break in either direction changes the base case [S4, S5]. Realised selling prices against the subsidised ceiling, because that spread is the franchise [S7]. Palm fresh-fruit-bunch prices and estate replanting activity, because they lead demand by a season [S8]. And any announcement from the state producer on NPK capacity commissioning, because that is the structural threat on the other side of the ledger [S10].

bear.narrative: Palm-estate economics stay squeezed: fresh fruit bunch prices near the levels smallholders report in 2026 keep estates cutting fertilisation frequency, while the subsidised NPK ceiling pulls what demand there is toward Pupuk Indonesia's cheaper bag. Sales growth goes four points below base and gross margin three points below, back under the FY2025 trough, so volume does not come and the raw-material basket is not recovered in price. Working capital is already at its peak and does not unwind: the receivables book owed by the long tail of plantation customers takes a Rp150bn impairment and the revolver stays drawn, so the balance sheet carries the peak stock for another year.

bull.narrative: The estate cycle turns: palm prices recover, replanting and fertilisation budgets reopen, and the Rp1,051bn of finished goods carried into the fourth quarter sells at full price. Sales growth runs four points above base and gross margin three points above, restoring the FY2023-24 spread as the imported nutrient basket is bought well and the premium oil-palm blends earn their price. The working-capital build unwinds by eight points of sales into cash and the payout is restored toward half of profit.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +10.4% is built from the actual: nine-month sales were Rp3,273.6bn, +12.0% on Rp2,923.8bn, target practice for the 7-8% full-year guidance management gave in December 2025 [S5, F11, F12, S6, F29]. We add a fourth quarter of Rp1,226bn, +6.5% on a weak Q4 2025, giving FY2026E sales near Rp4,500bn; that sits between the 9M run-rate and the company's own plan and is supported by Rp1,051bn of finished-goods stock carried at end-September, the largest Q4 ammunition the company has ever held [S5, F15]. FY2027E +7.0% is the company's guided growth rate applied forward, not a recovery assumption: the same slide deck the guidance comes from said the target depends on palm-estate demand holding up [S6]. From FY2028E we fade to +6.0%, +5.0% and +5.0% because the 700,000-tonne line was already 83% utilised in FY2025 and the only new project in the filings, Tanjung Buton, is land and site works, not a funded plant [S4, F5, F3]. The terminal rate of 4.0% is the house nominal rate.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the last actual, not on the better years: FY2025 gross margin was 21.27% (Rp866.8bn on Rp4,075.0bn) and the nine months to September 2026 ran 21.43% (Rp701.5bn on Rp3,273.6bn), so the margin has been stable through a year of falling then rising raw-material prices [S5, S4]. The 24.5% of FY2023-FY2024 was a wider raw-material spread that the 2025 result did not reproduce, and we do not assume it returns. We hold 21.4% for FY2026E and 21.5% thereafter in nominal terms, with the Brent link and partial pass-through doing the cost work. No margin recovery is capitalised.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Set to zero, deliberately. The chemicals registry defaults SAMF to Brent, but the observed 2026 record rejects that link: Brent carried a war premium through the year while SAMF's nine-month gross margin held at 21.4%, essentially the FY2025 level, because the raw-material basket is imported phosphate and potash plus nitrogen intermediates priced on fertiliser markets rather than on crude [S5, S10, F9]. Applying the deck's Brent path would have cut FY2026E gross margin to 18.6% against an actual 21.4% - a drift sourced from nothing. We therefore model the margin from the last actual and let the mined-nutrient cycle sit in the scenarios, where the downside is explicit.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Moot at a zero exposed share, and set to one so the engine applies no cost shock: every rupiah of raw-material cost change is carried in the gross-margin input itself, which is calibrated on the two most recent actual years [S5, S4]. The pass-through question is real - FY2025 showed it is partial - and it is tested in the bear case, where margin falls two points rather than being forced through a deck series that does not price NPK.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the last actual. Selling and general expenses were Rp372.5bn on Rp3,273.6bn of sales in the nine months to September 2026, 11.4%, against Rp444.8bn on Rp4,075.0bn (10.9%) in FY2025 [S5, S4]. The earlier 11.0% sat below the most recent actual with no source; the cost is mostly fixed distribution and salaries, so we carry 11.4% and assume no operating leverage either way.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack carries only the G&A depreciation line, Rp7.3bn, so history is restated from the LK: total depreciation was Rp42.7bn in FY2025 and Rp35.5bn in FY2024, and nine months of 2026 already ran Rp36.3bn, an annualised Rp48.4bn [S4, F1, F2, S5, F33]. On FY2026E sales of about Rp4,500bn that is 1.08%. We use 1.1% and hold it; the land revaluation added to the base but land is not depreciated, so the charge steps up only with the plant additions.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash capex was Rp61.8bn in FY2025 (1.5% of sales) and Rp189.8bn in FY2024, the year the Kalimantan capacity was finished; nine months of 2026 ran Rp28.2bn [S4, F31, S5]. With the 700,000-tonne line in place and the only identified project, Tanjung Buton, still at land and site-works stage, the most likely path is maintenance plus modest debottlenecking: 1.4% of sales, about Rp63bn, just above the restated depreciation charge, so the asset base is maintained rather than run down.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Rebuilt from the 30 September 2026 actual, not from the December 2025 balance sheet. Operating working capital at that date was Rp2,546.0bn - current assets Rp3,673.1bn less cash Rp236.2bn, less current liabilities Rp2,472.1bn net of current debt Rp1,581.2bn - against Rp1,723.7bn at 31 December 2025, a build of Rp822bn in nine months [S5, F15, F16, F14]. On FY2026E sales of Rp4,498.8bn that stock is 56.6% of revenue, and we hold it: no fourth-quarter unwind is assumed because none is sourced, and no further build either. The FY2026E net-debt line then reproduces the September actual of Rp1,311bn (F18 less F17) to within the interest convention, which charges interest on the December 2025 opening debt rather than on the drawn revolver [S5]. The unwind is the bull case's shock, not the base case's assumption.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax was Rp74.8bn on Rp342.3bn pre-tax profit, 21.9%, and the nine months of 2026 ran 21.8% [S0, S5]. We hold the statutory 22%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The September 2026 finance expense was Rp76.7bn for nine months, an annualised Rp102.3bn on average gross debt of about Rp1,200bn, roughly 8.5% [S5]. The disclosed Mandiri facilities price working-capital lines at 7.25-7.75% and investment credit at 7.75%, with LC and trust-receipt lines carrying fees on top [S5]. We use 8.5%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history; cash is a small share of the balance sheet and earns near-nothing, Rp0.4bn of finance income in nine months of 2026 [S5].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries the draw that has already happened, so the forecast debt line is gross debt on the full interest-bearing definition rather than the FY2025A opening balance left untouched. Total interest-bearing debt at 30 September 2026 was short-term bank loans Rp1,547.5bn [F18] plus current maturities of bank loans Rp29.9bn [F35] and finance liabilities Rp3.8bn [F36] plus non-current bank loans Rp62.0bn [F37] and finance liabilities Rp2.3bn [F38], Rp1,645.5bn in all, against Rp773.7bn at 31 December 2025; the net new borrowing of Rp871.8bn is the difference and matches the financing cash flow (proceeds 3,328.9 less repayments 2,430.6 less long-term repayments 22.4, net 816.0) plus the lease movement [S5]. From FY2027E the line is zero: the revolver stays drawn and the model repays nothing, which is the neutral financing assumption rather than a repayment plan. Net debt is unchanged by this input (net borrowing raises debt and cash together); what it fixes is the composition, so the forecast shows gross debt of Rp1,645.5bn and positive cash instead of a negative cash plug [S5].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero. Other income and expense are small and non-recurring; FY2026 had a Rp13.3bn other-expense line, mostly receivables impairments, and no repeatable item is capitalised [S5].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The three operating subsidiaries are 90.96%-95.45% owned, and minorities took Rp12.1bn of Rp267.5bn in FY2025, 4.5% [S4, S0]. We hold 4.5%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Held at the last actual. The FY2025 dividend was Rp10.5 a share, Rp107.6bn, 42.1% of attributable profit, declared at the 18 June 2026 AGMS [S5, F10, S0]. The two prior years paid about 49-50% [S4], but the board cut the payout in a year of negative free cash flow and the revolver is drawn; assuming it raises the payout it has just cut has no source. We hold 42.1% and let the restoration toward half be an upside case, not the base.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No issuance or buyback is disclosed; the 1:2 split in February 2025 changed the count, not the capital [S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House nominal terminal rate for the reporting currency, consistent with long-run Indonesian nominal GDP growth and below the nominal cost of capital. Reviewed against this company and kept: volume is capped by existing plant, the terminal margin is the last actual, and the rate sits under the nominal cost of capital, so the DCF does not capitalise growth that no funded project supports.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E is built off the Dec-2025 balance sheet, not the 30 Sep 2026 actuals: the model's FY2026E net debt is Rp781.3bn against Rp1,311.3bn actual (F18 1,547.5 less F17 236.2), and FY2026E delta-NWC is Rp300.7bn against the Rp822bn already incurred in 9M 2026 (NWC 1,723.7 to 2,546). The 45% ratio on FY2026E revenue implies year-end NWC of Rp2,024bn, i.e. an unstated Rp522bn Q4 release equal to 54% of Q4 COGS, while the report's own thesis is that this build may not unwind.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt FY2026E from the 30 September actual. nwc_pct went from 0.45 to 0.566 in every forecast year: operating working capital at 30 Sep 2026 was Rp2,546.0bn (current assets 3,673.1 less cash 236.2, less current liabilities 2,472.1 net of current debt 1,581.2) against 1,723.7 at Dec-2025. FY2026E NWC is now 2,546.3, delta-NWC 822.6 (the build already incurred, not 300.7), and the FY2026E net-debt line is 1,316.9 against the 1,311.3 actual (F18 less F17); the 5.6bn residual is the opening-debt interest convention, disclosed in section 3. No Q4 release is assumed. The DCF value per share fell from 191.3 to 157.1 (-17.9pct) on the NWC rebuild; the later +Rp299.6bn double-count bridge add-back (+Rp29.2/share) takes it to Rp186.3, the target to Rp177.4 and the return to -29.9pct. Rating SELL unchanged.

challenges.challenge: The P/E cross-check is described as '8.29 times our FY2026E earnings' but the model's metric is FY2025A net profit Rp255.4bn (EPS 24.9), giving 206.5; on FY2026E net profit Rp300.6bn (EPS 29.3) the same multiple gives 243.0, Rp36.5/share higher.
challenges.answer: Text corrected rather than the metric: the engine applies the multiple to LTM FY2025A attributable earnings (Rp255.4bn), not to our FY2026E forecast. Report section 4 now says so and justifies the audited-year basis (a peer multiple on our own forecast capitalises the estimate twice); the FY2026E implied P/E is still shown in the multiples table. P/E value 222.9 at 8.94x.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA metric is Rp429.3bn, the un-restated pack EBITDA (EBIT 422.0 plus G&A depreciation 7.3); the model's own restated FY2025A EBITDA is Rp464.7bn (F1/F2 total D&A 42.7). The Rp35.4bn COGS depreciation the report says it restated is missing from the multiple, understating the method by about Rp18/share (99.7 vs 81.4 at 5.25x).
challenges.answer: Added fact F34 (revenue FY2025A, audited financial highlights) to trigger the engine LTM restatement, so the EV/EBITDA metric is now the restated FY2025A EBITDA of Rp464.7bn (pack 429.3), carrying the Rp35.4bn COGS depreciation. EV/EBITDA value rose from 81.4 to Rp174.5 at the blended 6.26x after the restated EBITDA and the +Rp299.6bn bridge add-back.

challenges.challenge: 40% of the blend rests on peer-median multiples from a heterogeneous CHEMICALS set: the 5.25x EV/EBITDA median is AVIA (paint), alongside AGII (industrial gas), TPIA (petchem) and AKPI/APLI (plastics). SAMF's own four-year mean is 7.26x EV/EBITDA and 9.86x P/E; at own-history means the EV/EBITDA value is about 166, not 81. The 65% cross-check gap is explained qualitatively but never reconciled.
challenges.answer: Set valuation.multiple_source to blend, so each multiple is the average of the peer median and the SAMF own-history five-year mean, which is the honest treatment for a heterogeneous CHEMICALS set (paint, gas, petchem, plastics). EV/EBITDA uses 6.26x (5.25 peer, 7.26 own) and P/E 8.94x. EV/EBITDA value Rp174.5, P/E Rp222.8; the EV/EBITDA cross-check is now 6.3pct below the DCF (was 65pct).

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says 'working capital is already at its peak, so the revolver stays drawn and the interest bill rises', but the bear shocks are only revenue_growth -4pp and gross_margin -2pp; there is no nwc_pct shock and net_borrowing is zero in every year. The bear does not model its own thesis.
challenges.answer: The bear now shocks its own thesis: a.nwc_pct +0.08 (the build does not unwind) alongside revenue growth -4pp, gross margin -3pp and a Rp150bn receivables impairment. On the current model — after the +Rp299.6bn bridge — the bear v0 is Rp121.4 and the bear target Rp136.2; the earlier 96.6/107.8 predate the bridge.

challenges.challenge: No credit-loss, inventory write-down or equity-raise case is modelled. Receivables are owed by 500+ plantation customers under documented cost stress [S8], finished goods are Rp1,051bn, and FCFE is negative with a Rp1,548bn revolver; a rights issue or impairment is a live downside that appears nowhere.
challenges.answer: Modelled the credit-loss case: the bear carries a one-sided a.other_nonop -150 receivables impairment, sourced to the 500-plus plantation customers under documented cost stress and the impairments already booked. The dilutive rights-issue case is described in section 5 as the tail beyond the bear and not modelled, because no facility is disclosed as at risk; the asymmetry is justified in qc_justifications (scenario.mirror).

challenges.challenge: The bull adds +2pp gross margin, leaving 23.5%, still below the 24.5% actually earned in FY2023-24 which the report refuses to restore, and +4pp growth on a base that fades to 5% despite 700kt capacity against 581kt output (17% idle, no capex needed). The 'bull' is a mid-case.
challenges.answer: Bull gross margin +0.03 to the FY2023 and FY2024 level of 24.5pct, revenue growth +4pp on the 700kt line against 581kt output, and a.nwc_pct -0.08. On the current model the bull v0 is Rp316.2 and the twelve-month bull target Rp342.1 before the liquidity haircut (Rp273.7 post-haircut, above the Rp270 price); the earlier 291.4/316.8 predate the +Rp299.6bn bridge. The spare capacity is stated in sections 1 and 5.

challenges.challenge: The report names Q4 cash conversion and an inventory unwind as the signpost that would raise its target, yet the bull scenario contains no working-capital relief: its shocks are revenue and margin only. The single most likely upside catalyst is absent from the upside case.
challenges.answer: Bull now carries a.nwc_pct -0.08, the working-capital relief the report names as its own signpost. With margin, growth and the relief, the bull v0 is Rp316.2 and the twelve-month bull target Rp342.1 before the liquidity haircut on the current model.

challenges.challenge: A 20% liquidity discount is applied to the probability-weighted value and to every scenario, including the bull. It is at the top of the house range (RMKO and DOID carry 10%) and is unsourced against any ADV/float grid; it alone accounts for 42 of the 100-point gap to the Rp270 price (212 to 170). At 10% the target is 191 and the expected return -24.6%.
challenges.answer: The 20pct is not an analyst choice: it is the house coverage liquidity grid, which sets 20pct for ADTV below Rp500m and 10pct only below Rp2bn. The SAMF three-month ADTV is Rp182m, in the 20pct bucket; RMKO (Rp1.94bn) and DOID (Rp1.13bn) sit in the 10pct bucket, which is why they carry 10pct. Applying 10pct here would breach the grid and would require editing config, which the desk may not do. The grid is applied mechanically to every name; no change. On the current model the 20pct haircut is Rp44 of the Rp93 gap from the weighted Rp221.7 to the Rp177.4 target; at 10pct the target would be Rp199.5 and the return -26.1pct, so the rating does not turn on the grid.

challenges.challenge: params_basis states 'we set the exposed share at 35%' but link1_share is 0.0 and link1_pass 1.0, so the Brent deck is entirely unused and the documented treatment contradicts the input. Either the 35% exposure is real and the margin path should carry it, or the basis text is wrong.
challenges.answer: params_basis rewritten: the link is fully disabled, link1_share 0.0, and the text now says so and gives the reason (the observed 2026 record rejects the Brent link; the whole raw-material exposure sits in the gross-margin input and the mined-nutrient cycle in the scenarios). The contradictory 35pct sentence is gone.

challenges.challenge: The claim that inventory days rose 'from about 88 to about 111' is not reproducible: FY2025 inventory Rp866.8bn on COGS Rp3,208.2bn is 98.6 days, and 30 Sep 2026 inventory Rp1,744.8bn on annualised 9M COGS Rp3,429.5bn is 185.7 days. The figure is used to justify the 45% NWC input.

(i) The accruals ratio is a single 9M-2026 measure (about 22pct on average total assets) with no three-year trend, although the card says the trend matters more than the level. challenges.answer: Delivered the full EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS output contract. The accruals ratio is therefore about 11.6pct, 3.0pct and -1.5pct across the three audited years: the 9M-2026 figure of about 22.0pct is a break in a two-year clean trend, not a persistent pattern, which is why we classify it optics-class.
